# 5. SYNOPSIS
## 5.1 Title of Project UrbanBites - A Comprehensive Food Delivery and Restaurant Management Platform
## 5.2 Introduction In the contemporary digital ecosystem, the food service industry relies heavily on online aggregation platforms to bridge the gap between culinary providers and consumers. The real-world problem this project addresses is the fragmented nature of traditional restaurant operations, where businesses struggle to manage dine-in, takeaway, and digital orders simultaneously without incurring exorbitant commission fees from third-party monopolies. UrbanBites introduces a unified, scalable platform that empowers end-users to seamlessly discover local cuisines, while providing robust, independent management suites for restaurant owners, delivery dispatchers, and system administrators.
Existing solutions often fail to provide sufficient transparency and real-time synchronization between the restaurant's kitchen, the delivery fleet, and the waiting customer. Small-to-medium restaurant owners frequently lack access to detailed analytics and real-time inventory management, resulting in order fulfillment delays and diminished customer satisfaction. Furthermore, many existing platforms utilize legacy architectures that suffer from latency during high-traffic meal hours, leading to dropped carts and broken payment flows.
UrbanBites solves this multi-faceted problem by implementing a highly responsive, event-driven architecture using modern full-stack technologies. By utilizing a React-based dynamic frontend and a Spring Boot microservice-oriented backend, the system guarantees low-latency communications and reliable state persistence. The platform is designed for a tripartite target audience: consumers seeking a premium ordering experience, restaurant partners requiring granular control over their digital menus and operations, and delivery personnel seeking optimized dispatch routing and instantaneous order assignments.
## 5.3 Objectives - To design and implement a secure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) system ensuring authenticated interactions for Users, Restaurant Owners, Delivery Agents, and Administrators. - To develop a dynamic, location-aware Restaurant Discovery module that allows users to filter, search, and view geographically relevant culinary options. - To build a highly responsive, state-managed Cart and Checkout pipeline that calculates taxes, dynamic delivery fees, and order totals in real-time. - To engineer a dedicated Restaurant Partner Dashboard facilitating real-time menu management, order acceptance workflows, and inventory tracking. - To establish a bidirectional WebSocket communication layer for real-time delivery tracking and instantaneous status updates across all user interfaces. - To formulate a robust Pricing Engine Service on the backend to prevent frontend manipulation and ensure absolute data integrity during financial transactions. - To create an independent Delivery Agent interface optimized for mobile devices, enabling personnel to manage their availability, receive dispatch alerts, and confirm deliveries. - To construct a comprehensive Administrative Panel for platform governance, including user verification, restaurant onboarding approvals, and system-wide analytics. - To ensure responsive User Interface (UI) design utilizing modern CSS frameworks, guaranteeing cross-device compatibility from desktop monitors to smartphone screens. - To deploy the application using modern cloud-hosting platforms, establishing continuous integration pipelines and environment-specific configuration management.

# 6. FEATURES AND FUNCTIONALITIES
## 6.1 Centralized Role-Based Authentication The authentication mechanism serves as the primary gateway to the application, distinguishing between four distinct user roles: Consumer, Restaurant Owner, Delivery Agent, and Admin. Internally, this feature relies on JSON Web Tokens (JWT) generated by the Spring Security framework. Upon successful login, the server issues a cryptographically signed token containing the user's role hierarchy, which the frontend intercepts and stores securely. This ensures that users are immediately routed to their respective dashboards while strictly preventing unauthorized access to administrative or partner-level endpoints, thereby safeguarding the platform's sensitive business operations.
## 6.2 Intelligent Restaurant and Menu Discovery This feature empowers consumers to browse a vast repository of restaurants categorized by cuisine, ratings, and operational status. The internal mechanism utilizes JPA repository queries on the backend to dynamically fetch active restaurants based on user parameters, rendering them via reusable React components. It benefits the user by minimizing cognitive load; they can effortlessly search for specific dishes or establishments using real-time search filters without experiencing page reloads, resulting in a highly engaging and fluid browsing experience.
## 6.3 Real-Time Persistent Cart Management The application features a non-volatile shopping cart that persists state across different application routes and browsing sessions. Internally, the frontend utilizes React Context API combined with local storage synchronization to maintain cart data, while validating item availability and price alterations through the backend `PricingEngineService`. This feature provides immense value to the user by preventing data loss if the browser is accidentally closed, and it strictly prevents cross-restaurant ordering conflicts by automatically clearing or warning the user when attempting to add items from disparate locations.
## 6.4 Secure and Transparent Checkout Pipeline The checkout pipeline is designed to transform the cart contents into a finalized, actionable order while maintaining absolute transparency regarding cost breakdowns. How it works internally involves the React `CartPage` submitting an order payload to the backend `OrderController`, where it undergoes strict validation before being persisted into the MySQL database. It benefits the user by clearly displaying base item costs, calculated taxes, and dynamically generated delivery fees before confirming the purchase, eliminating hidden charges and fostering trust in the platform.
## 6.5 Dedicated Restaurant Management Dashboard This isolated suite provides restaurant owners with comprehensive tools to oversee their digital storefront. Internally, the dashboard interacts with protected API endpoints allowing owners to perform CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on their `menu_items` and `menu_categories` tables, while simultaneously listening for incoming order notifications. This feature is critical as it digitizes the traditional restaurant workflow, allowing owners to toggle dish availability instantly if ingredients run out, thereby preventing unfulfillable orders and customer dissatisfaction.
## 6.6 Delivery Agent Dispatch and Logistics Console A specialized module built to manage the logistics of the delivery fleet. Internally, this feature connects the delivery agent's profile status to the `DispatchService`, broadcasting their geographical coordinates and online availability to the central server. When a restaurant prepares an order, the system assigns it to an available agent, triggering a UI prompt for acceptance. This heavily benefits the logistical operations of the platform by minimizing manual intervention, ensuring that food is collected and dispatched optimally based on real-time driver availability.
## 6.7 Real-Time Order Status and Tracking This feature provides consumers with live visibility into the lifecycle of their order, from kitchen preparation to final delivery. Technically, it leverages a WebSocket integration layer established between the Spring Boot server and the React frontend, pushing asynchronous events whenever a partner updates an order state. The primary benefit is user peace of mind; customers are kept informed instantaneously without needing to refresh their browser, significantly reducing customer support inquiries regarding order locations.
## 6.8 Platform Administration and Governance An overarching administrative dashboard designed for the platform owners to monitor the entire ecosystem. Internally, it queries aggregated data from multiple database tables, allowing the admin to approve or reject pending Delivery Agent registrations and Restaurant partner applications via the `AdminService`. This feature acts as the quality assurance gatekeeper for the platform, ensuring that only verified entities operate within the marketplace and maintaining the overall integrity and safety of the service.

# 8. MODULES DESCRIPTION
## 1. Authentication and Security Module The Authentication module is the foundational layer responsible for identity verification and access control. Its primary purpose is to ensure that only registered and verified users can interact with the platform's protected resources. Technically, it involves the `AuthController` on the backend receiving credentials, verifying them against encrypted hashes in the database using `BCryptPasswordEncoder`, and issuing a signed JWT. On the frontend, a React Context provider intercepts this token, persisting it in local storage and attaching it to the headers of subsequent Axios requests. The input is user credentials (email/password), and the output is a secure session state unlocking specific routed dashboards based on the user's encoded role.
## 2. Consumer Experience and Shopping Module This module handles the entire B2C (Business-to-Consumer) workflow, allowing end-users to discover food and place orders. Its purpose is to provide a frictionless shopping experience. It operates via React components mapping over data arrays fetched from the `RestaurantController` and `MenuController`. The Cart state is managed globally, accumulating items until the user initiates the checkout process. During checkout, the frontend submits the cart payload, which the backend `PricingEngineService` recalculates to ensure data integrity before persisting. Inputs include search queries, category filters, and cart additions; outputs include dynamically rendered restaurant lists, cart summaries, and finalized order confirmations.
## 3. Restaurant Operations Module Designed exclusively for culinary partners, this module facilitates digital restaurant management. The purpose is to allow owners to control their public profile, menu offerings, and daily order queues. Technically, it involves restricted endpoints where the owner's ID must match the database entity being modified. The dashboard features CRUD interfaces for `MenuItem` entities and a live WebSocket listener for the `Orders` table. When an order arrives, the owner interacts with the UI to update the status (e.g., from 'PENDING' to 'PREPARING'). Inputs comprise menu data entry and order status toggles, resulting in real-time database updates and synchronous notifications dispatched to the waiting consumer.
## 4. Delivery and Dispatch Module This logistical module orchestrates the physical transportation of orders. Its purpose is to assign active delivery agents to prepared orders and track their progress. It works by utilizing a `DispatchService` that monitors the `DeliveryAgentProfile` statuses. Once an admin approves an agent, they can toggle their status to 'ONLINE'. The system algorithmically matches available agents to pending deliveries based on regional parameters. Inputs include the agent's live availability status and order acceptance triggers; the output is a coordinated workflow that updates the main order entity, linking the agent's ID to the customer's purchase and initiating the final delivery phase.
## 5. Administrative Oversight Module The Administrative module is the central command center for the platform operators. Its purpose is to govern user registrations, approve business partners, and resolve system anomalies. Technically, it interacts with the `AdminService` and corresponding controllers to query aggregate platform statistics and modify crucial flags (e.g., changing a delivery agent's `is_verified` status to true). It bypasses standard constraints to view all data across the ecosystem. Inputs are administrative commands and approval actions; outputs are global state changes that unblock pending users or suspend fraudulent accounts, ensuring platform stability.

# 9. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
## Presentation Layer The Presentation Layer forms the topmost tier of the architecture, built predominantly with React.js and styled using Tailwind CSS. It is responsible for rendering the user interfaces, managing client-side routing via React Router, and capturing user interactions. This layer utilizes Context API for state management, particularly for authentication tokens and cart data. It abstracts the complexity of the backend by presenting data in an intuitive, responsive format across various device resolutions, while intercepting UI events to trigger asynchronous HTTP requests.
## Controller Layer Sitting at the edge of the backend micro-architecture, the Controller Layer handles all incoming HTTP requests routed from the Presentation layer. Built with Spring Web MVC annotations (e.g., `@RestController`, `@RequestMapping`), this layer acts as the initial entry point. It is responsible for deserializing incoming JSON payloads into Java Data Transfer Objects (DTOs), validating basic structural constraints (such as null checks), and routing the validated data to the appropriate Service Layer components. It subsequently formats the service responses back into HTTP JSON responses with appropriate status codes (e.g., 200 OK, 400 Bad Request).
## Service Layer The Service Layer is the core analytical engine of the application where all complex business rules and validations reside. Annotated with `@Service`, components like `OrderService`, `PricingEngineService`, and `DispatchService` process data detached from the HTTP context. This layer executes crucial logic, such as recalculating cart totals to prevent client-side spoofing, matching delivery agents to orders, and verifying user permissions before executing database mutations. It ensures that the application's domain logic is centralized, testable, and completely independent of the web controllers.
## Data Access Layer (DAO) The Data Access Layer interfaces directly with the database to perform all persistent data operations. Utilizing Spring Data JPA, this layer abstracts raw SQL queries into programmatic interfaces. By extending `JpaRepository`, it provides automatic implementation for standard CRUD operations and allows for the creation of complex custom queries using method naming conventions or `@Query` annotations. This layer translates the object-oriented Java models into relational database records, ensuring smooth data serialization and deserialization.
## Database Layer The foundational layer of the architecture is the Database Layer, powered by a relational database management system (MySQL). This layer enforces absolute data integrity through strict schemas, foreign key constraints, and relational mappings. It houses normalized tables such as `users`, `restaurants`, `menu_items`, and `orders`. By maintaining ACID properties, this layer ensures that critical transactions, particularly multi-step order placements and status updates, are committed reliably without data corruption.
## External Services Layer This layer handles integration with third-party APIs and external cloud infrastructure. It encompasses the deployment pipelines hosted on platforms like Vercel and Render, ensuring the application is accessible via public domains. Furthermore, this layer manages CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) configurations to allow secure communication between the separately hosted frontend and backend. It may also encapsulate any external email providers, payment gateways, or cloud storage solutions required to extend the core platform's capabilities.
## Complete Request-Response Flow When a user executes an action, such as submitting a checkout request, the flow initiates in the browser where the React Presentation Layer constructs a JSON payload containing the cart details. This payload is transmitted via an Axios POST request to the Spring Boot Controller Layer. The `OrderController` intercepts the request, validates the DTO, and passes it to the `OrderService`. The Service Layer then invokes the `PricingEngineService` to recalculate the exact cost using data fetched via the Data Access Layer from the Database Layer. Once the business logic validates the transaction, the DAO saves the new `Order` entity into the MySQL database. Upon successful persistence, the Service Layer triggers a WebSocket event to notify the target restaurant. Finally, the Controller Layer returns a 201 Created HTTP response to the frontend, which parses the response and updates the UI to display the order success screen to the user.

# 10. ABSTRACT
The exponential growth of the digital food delivery industry necessitates platforms that are not only user-friendly but structurally robust enough to handle complex, multi-party logistical operations. **UrbanBites** is a comprehensive, full-stack food delivery and restaurant management system designed to seamlessly integrate the experiences of consumers, culinary businesses, and delivery personnel into a unified digital ecosystem. Built utilizing a modern technological stack, the application employs React.js with Tailwind CSS for a highly responsive, state-driven frontend, and Java Spring Boot for a scalable, RESTful micro-architecture backend, all persisting data within a relational MySQL database.
The platform features a strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) mechanism governed by stateless JWT authentication, ensuring secure routing across four distinct administrative interfaces. Key functionalities include dynamic geographic restaurant discovery, an immutable real-time cart system, and an algorithmic pricing engine to guarantee transactional integrity. For logistical operations, UrbanBites implements a sophisticated dispatch module coupled with WebSocket technology to provide instantaneous order status updates and delivery tracking, eliminating the reliance on inefficient HTTP polling. The system architecture follows a strict separation of concerns, utilizing MVC patterns to isolate presentation logic from complex service-layer business rules and data access objects. Ultimately, UrbanBites demonstrates the practical application of enterprise-grade software engineering principles to solve real-world aggregation challenges, resulting in a production-ready system that drastically improves operational efficiency for restaurants while delivering a premium, transparent ordering experience for end-users.
---
# 11. DETAILED INTRODUCTION
The contemporary food service landscape has undergone a paradigm shift, transitioning from traditional dine-in and phone-based ordering to predominantly digital, application-driven ecosystems. In today's fast-paced world, consumers demand instant access to diverse culinary options, coupled with complete transparency regarding pricing and delivery logistics. Simultaneously, restaurant owners face the daunting challenge of digitizing their menus, managing online order queues, and coordinating with independent delivery fleets without disrupting their physical operations. This broader context highlights the absolute necessity for unified platforms capable of aggregating these disparate services into a single, cohesive marketplace. UrbanBites was conceived to directly address this industry-wide demand, providing a sophisticated technological bridge between local food vendors and the digital consumer base.
Despite the proliferation of massive food delivery conglomerates, existing solutions often present significant limitations, particularly for small to medium-sized restaurant enterprises. Many traditional tools and manual approaches involve fragmented communication—where a restaurant might receive an order via a tablet, manually punch it into a point-of-sale system, and then physically coordinate with a separate delivery service. These disconnected workflows lead to high error rates, delayed deliveries, and an inability to track data analytics effectively. Furthermore, third-party platforms frequently enforce exorbitant commission structures and offer rigid interfaces that strip restaurant owners of control over their brand presentation and real-time menu availability, leading to immense friction in the B2B sector.
UrbanBites bridges this critical gap by offering a fully integrated, multi-portal architecture tailored to the specific needs of all involved stakeholders. By equipping consumers with an intuitive discovery and checkout application, while simultaneously provisioning restaurant owners and delivery agents with dedicated management dashboards, the project eliminates operational silos. Features such as real-time WebSocket notifications ensure that the moment a restaurant prepares a meal, a delivery agent is automatically dispatched, and the consumer is instantly notified. This level of synchronization replaces manual coordination with programmatic efficiency, empowering local restaurants to operate with the logistical sophistication of large-scale enterprises.
From an academic and technical perspective, building UrbanBites served as a comprehensive exercise in advanced full-stack software engineering. The project demonstrates proficiency in orchestrating a diverse array of modern technologies, transitioning from the declarative UI paradigms of React to the robust, object-oriented service architectures of Spring Boot. Developing this system required overcoming complex challenges such as managing asynchronous state across disparate client devices, securing REST endpoints against unauthorized manipulation, and designing normalized relational databases capable of handling complex transaction histories. Ultimately, the student learned how to architect a scalable application from conceptual database modeling to cloud-based production deployment, acquiring skills that are directly translatable to enterprise software development environments.

# 12. DETAILED OBJECTIVES
1. **To engineer a secure, token-based authentication system:** The system must implement JSON Web Tokens (JWT) through Spring Security to handle stateless user sessions. This objective is critical to ensure that sensitive endpoints are protected, and that users are strictly confined to actions permitted by their designated roles (Consumer, Owner, Agent, Admin). 2. **To develop a dynamic Restaurant Discovery interface:** The frontend must utilize React components to render a searchable, filterable grid of culinary partners fetched dynamically from the database. This allows users to easily navigate massive datasets of restaurants without experiencing page reloads, enhancing overall user retention. 3. **To implement a robust, persistent Cart Management module:** The application must utilize Context API to maintain cart state across various routes, synchronized seamlessly with local storage. This ensures that users do not lose their selected items if the application is refreshed, providing a frictionless shopping experience. 4. **To build an immutable server-side Pricing Engine:** All cart totals, taxes, and delivery fees must be recalculated exclusively on the Spring Boot backend prior to order confirmation. This technical approach is paramount to prevent malicious client-side manipulation of prices and ensure absolute financial data integrity. 5. **To construct a comprehensive Restaurant Partner Dashboard:** Restaurant owners must be provided with a protected suite to execute real-time CRUD operations on their digital menus. This empowers businesses to instantly update dish availability, preventing the logistical nightmare of receiving orders for out-of-stock items. 6. **To establish real-time order synchronization via WebSockets:** The architecture must depart from traditional HTTP polling by integrating a WebSocket layer for instantaneous event broadcasting. This enables the platform to push order status changes directly to the consumer and delivery agent instantly, drastically improving system responsiveness. 7. **To create an efficient Delivery Agent Dispatch logic:** The backend `DispatchService` must manage agent availability states and connect them to pending orders. By automating the linkage between a prepared order and an online agent, the system minimizes logistical bottlenecks and accelerates delivery times. 8. **To design a centralized Administrative Governance panel:** Administrators must have access to a master dashboard capable of viewing aggregated data and toggling verification flags (e.g., approving a pending delivery agent). This objective is necessary to maintain quality control and secure the platform from unverified entities. 9. **To ensure a fully responsive, mobile-first UI architecture:** The frontend must be styled utilizing Tailwind CSS utility classes to guarantee that the application adapts fluidly to mobile phones, tablets, and desktop monitors. Given that food ordering is highly mobile-centric, this objective is critical for market viability. 10. **To execute a production-ready cloud deployment strategy:** The application must be successfully deployed utilizing modern cloud infrastructure, specifically hosting the React frontend on Vercel and the Spring Boot API on Render. This demonstrates the ability to manage environment variables, CORS configurations, and continuous delivery pipelines in a real-world scenario.

# 13. TECHNOLOGIES USED (Detailed)
## 13.1 React.js React.js is an open-source, front-end JavaScript library utilized for building component-based user interfaces. It utilizes a Virtual DOM to optimize rendering performance, updating only the specific UI elements that have changed rather than reloading the entire HTML page. In this project, React powers the entirety of the frontend application, from the consumer-facing shopping interface to the complex partner dashboards. It was specifically chosen because its declarative component architecture allows for massive code reusability; for instance, the same `RestaurantCard` component can be utilized on the home page, search results, and favorite lists, significantly reducing development time.
## 13.2 Spring Boot Spring Boot is an extension of the Java Spring framework that drastically simplifies the setup and development of enterprise applications by providing opinionated default configurations. In UrbanBites, Spring Boot serves as the robust backend engine, exposing RESTful API endpoints via web controllers and managing complex business logic within its service layer. It was selected because of its unmatched dependency injection capabilities, strict typing, and seamless integration with the Java ecosystem, which provides a highly structured, scalable, and secure foundation necessary for handling financial data and multi-role authentications.
## 13.3 MySQL MySQL is a widely adopted, open-source Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) based on Structured Query Language. It structures data into interconnected tables, enforcing data integrity through schemas and foreign keys. In this application, MySQL houses all persistent state, encompassing user credentials, complex menu hierarchies, and historical order transactions. It was the right choice for this project due to its ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) compliance; food delivery applications process complex, multi-table updates during checkout, and a relational database guarantees that an order is never recorded if the corresponding payment or item data fails to save.
## 13.4 Spring Security & JWT Spring Security is a powerful, highly customizable authentication and access-control framework, while JSON Web Tokens (JWT) represent a standard for securely transmitting information as a JSON object. Specifically, UrbanBites utilizes this combination to implement stateless session management. Upon login, the server encrypts user roles into a JWT, which the client attaches to subsequent requests to access protected endpoints like the `/admin/dashboard`. This architecture was chosen because it allows the backend API to remain entirely stateless, conserving server memory and allowing the application to scale horizontally without worrying about session replication across servers.
## 13.5 WebSockets WebSocket is an advanced communication protocol providing full-duplex, bi-directional communication channels over a single TCP connection. In the context of UrbanBites, WebSockets are utilized to bypass the limitations of traditional HTTP requests, which require the client to constantly ask the server for updates. Instead, when a restaurant owner accepts an order, the server instantly pushes this event through the WebSocket connection to the consumer's tracking screen. This technology was crucial to implement because real-time feedback is non-negotiable in the logistics industry, and relying on HTTP polling would heavily overload the backend servers during peak traffic.
## 13.6 Tailwind CSS Tailwind CSS is a highly popular utility-first CSS framework that provides low-level styling classes directly within HTML/JSX markup, rather than relying on external, monolithic stylesheet files. Throughout UrbanBites, Tailwind is responsible for the entire visual design system, dictating typography, spacing, colors, and responsive breakpoints. It was chosen because it allows developers to build custom, bespoke interfaces rapidly without context-switching between JavaScript and CSS files, ensuring that the final product adheres to a modern, vibrant aesthetic while remaining perfectly responsive on mobile devices.

# 14. SYSTEM MODULES (Detailed)
## 1. The Authentication and Identity Module The Authentication module forms the secure perimeter of the application. The workflow is triggered when a user submits credentials via the Login or Registration forms on the frontend. This action constructs an HTTP POST request targeting the backend `AuthController`. The backend processes this by delegating to the `AuthenticationManager`, which compares the provided raw password against the BCrypt-hashed string stored in the `users` database table. If validation succeeds, a signed JWT containing the user's role and ID is generated and returned. Validation rules strictly check for email uniqueness during registration and enforce password complexity. The final output to the user is a seamless redirection to their role-specific dashboard (e.g., routing an Admin to the global overview, and a Consumer to the home discovery page) while storing the token securely in the browser's local storage.
## 2. The Consumer Discovery and Ordering Module This module encompasses the core shopping experience. User actions such as typing in a search bar or clicking "Add to Cart" trigger immediate responses. Browsing triggers the frontend to fetch data via the `RestaurantController`, reading from the `restaurants` and `menu_items` tables. When a user adds an item, the React Context updates the cart array in memory. Upon initiating checkout, the payload is dispatched to the `OrderController`. The critical backend processing occurs within the `PricingEngineService`, which ignores frontend prices, queries the database for the true `unit_price` of each item, calculates platform taxes, and verifies inventory availability. If validation passes, records are written to the `orders` and `order_items` tables. The output shown to the user is a transition from the checkout drawer to a dedicated "Order Success" screen, providing them with an immutable digital receipt.
## 3. The Restaurant Partner Management Module Designed for B2B interactions, this module is triggered when a user with the `RESTAURANT_OWNER` role accesses their dashboard. The owner can initiate actions such as "Add New Menu Item" or "Toggle Availability". These actions hit endpoints protected by Spring Security, which first verifies that the authenticated token matches the owner of the target restaurant. The backend logic then performs CRUD operations against the `menu_items` table. Furthermore, the dashboard maintains an active WebSocket subscription. When a consumer completes the checkout module, the backend publishes a message to this channel, triggering the dashboard to dynamically render a new incoming order card. The owner can then click "Accept Order", which updates the `orders` table status and broadcasts the change back to the consumer. The visual output for the owner is a highly organized Kanban-style board reflecting real-time kitchen obligations.
## 4. The Logistical Dispatch Module This module oversees the physical delivery phase. It is triggered by a delivery agent toggling their status to "Online" on their mobile-optimized dashboard, and subsequently by a restaurant marking an order as "Ready for Pickup". The backend `DispatchService` continually monitors the `delivery_agents` table. When an order requires an agent, the service executes logic to identify agents where `is_online = true` and `is_verified = true`. Once assigned, a push notification is sent to the specific agent's interface. Validation rules ensure an agent cannot accept multiple active orders simultaneously unless explicitly permitted by batching rules. When the agent clicks "Confirm Delivery", the backend updates the order status to 'DELIVERED', finalizes the transaction timestamp, and updates the UI for all parties, displaying a successful completion screen to the consumer.
## 5. The Administrative Governance Module The Administrative module operates at the highest privilege level, triggered when the platform owner logs into the Admin panel. Actions here include "Approve Restaurant Application" or "Verify Delivery Agent". The backend `AdminService` bypasses standard user constraints, executing wide-ranging read operations across all tables to compile systemic statistics. A notable backend process involves correcting the delivery agent approval flow; when an admin clicks "Approve", the logic ensures the `DeliveryAgentProfile`'s `is_verified` flag is definitively set to true, resolving complex states where agents were perpetually stuck in pending status. Database writes primarily involve updating boolean flags on user profiles. The output is a comprehensive, data-rich table view allowing the admin to visually confirm the updated verification statuses of all platform partners.

# 15. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (Detailed Layer-wise)
## Specific Use Case Walkthrough: The Checkout Flow To fully understand the architecture, tracing the "Checkout" flow provides the clearest example of layer interactions. 1. **Presentation Layer:** The user clicks "Confirm Payment" on the React `CartPage.jsx`. The frontend aggregates the cart items and the user's JWT into an Axios POST request. 2. **Controller Layer:** The Spring Boot `OrderController` receives the payload. It deserializes the JSON into an `OrderRequestDTO` and validates basic annotations (e.g., ensuring `menuItemIds` is not empty). 3. **Service Layer:** The controller passes the DTO to the `OrderService`. The service retrieves the User entity based on the JWT context. It then delegates to the `PricingEngineService`, which independently queries the database to ascertain current item prices, completely ignoring client-provided costs to prevent manipulation. 4. **Data Access Layer & Database:** The `OrderRepository` and `OrderItemRepository` are invoked to execute `save()` operations, writing the validated total, status (PENDING), and item mappings into the MySQL `orders` and `order_items` tables within a single transactional boundary. 5. **External Services / WebSockets:** Upon successful database commit, the `OrderService` triggers a message to the WebSocket broker, broadcasting an alert to the specific restaurant owner's connected client. 6. **Return Flow:** The Controller formats an `OrderResponseDTO` and sends a 201 Created HTTP response. The React application receives this, clears the local Context cart state, and utilizes React Router to redirect the user to the `OrderSuccessPage`.
## Security Architecture The platform's security is strictly governed by a stateless JWT paradigm. The Presentation layer handles security by utilizing Higher-Order Components (HOCs) or protected route wrappers that inspect the local token; if absent, the user is forced to the login screen. On the backend, Spring Security intercepts all incoming requests at the filter chain level. It extracts the JWT from the `Authorization: Bearer` header, cryptographically verifies the signature using a hidden server secret, and unpacks the user's roles. Endpoints are secured utilizing method-level annotations (e.g., `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")`). Data flows between the frontend and backend are exclusively encrypted over HTTPS/TLS, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks from intercepting sensitive credentials or payment payloads.
## External Services and Cloud Integration The architecture extends beyond the local environment by integrating with external cloud services. The frontend React application is deployed to Vercel, which provides a globally distributed Edge Network for rapid asset delivery and handles automated domain routing. The Spring Boot backend is hosted on Render, operating as an always-on web service. Connecting these two disparate environments requires strict Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) configurations within the Controller layer, explicitly whitelisting the Vercel production domain to allow API communication while blocking malicious external domains. This layered approach ensures high availability, automated continuous integration, and distinct separation between static asset serving and dynamic API processing.
---
# 16. DATABASE DESIGN
The database architecture is structured relationally using MySQL to enforce strict data integrity across the platform's multi-faceted operations.
### 1. Users Table This table is the central identity repository for the application. It stores the authentication credentials and profile information for all individuals accessing the system, regardless of their role. It is heavily referenced by almost every other entity in the database.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `user_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique identifier for the user. | | `full_name` | VARCHAR(100) | NOT NULL | The user's complete name. | | `email` | VARCHAR(150) | UNIQUE, NOT NULL | Primary email used for login and notifications. | | `password_hash` | VARCHAR(255) | NOT NULL | BCrypt encrypted string of the user's password. | | `role` | ENUM | NOT NULL | Defines access level (USER, ADMIN, RESTAURANT_OWNER, DELIVERY_AGENT). | | `created_at` | TIMESTAMP | DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP | Record creation time for auditing. |
### 2. Restaurants Table This table stores the public profile and operational metadata for food establishments. It is vital for the discovery module and acts as the parent entity for all menu items.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `restaurant_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique identifier for the restaurant. | | `owner_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (users.user_id) | Links the establishment to a specific owner account. | | `name` | VARCHAR(150) | NOT NULL | The public name of the restaurant. | | `address` | TEXT | NOT NULL | The physical location for delivery routing. | | `image_url` | VARCHAR(255) | NULL | URL referencing the establishment's banner image. | | `is_active` | BOOLEAN | DEFAULT TRUE | Toggle allowing owners to temporarily hide their store. |
### 3. MenuItems Table This table catalogues the individual culinary offerings available at each restaurant. It is queried heavily by the cart and pricing engines.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `item_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique identifier for the specific dish. | | `restaurant_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (restaurants.restaurant_id) | Links the item to its providing restaurant. | | `name` | VARCHAR(100) | NOT NULL | Name of the dish (e.g., "Spicy Chicken Burger"). | | `price` | DECIMAL(10,2) | NOT NULL | Base cost of the item used in checkout calculations. | | `is_available` | BOOLEAN | DEFAULT TRUE | Allows owners to mark items out of stock instantly. |
### 4. Orders Table The most critical transactional table in the system, it records the complete lifecycle of a consumer's purchase, bridging the user, restaurant, and delivery agent.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `order_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique identifier for the transaction. | | `user_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (users.user_id) | The consumer who placed the order. | | `restaurant_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (restaurants.restaurant_id)| The establishment fulfilling the order. | | `agent_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY, NULLABLE | The delivery personnel assigned (null until dispatched). | | `total_amount` | DECIMAL(10,2) | NOT NULL | The final calculated cost including taxes/fees. | | `status` | VARCHAR(50) | NOT NULL | Current state (PENDING, PREPARING, DELIVERED). |
### 5. OrderItems Table This table resolves the many-to-many relationship between Orders and MenuItems, recording exactly what was purchased within a specific transaction at a historical price point.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `order_item_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique mapping identifier. | | `order_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (orders.order_id) | The parent order this item belongs to. | | `item_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (menu_items.item_id) | The specific dish ordered. | | `quantity` | INT | NOT NULL | Number of units purchased. | | `unit_price` | DECIMAL(10,2) | NOT NULL | Locked price at the time of purchase to prevent historical corruption. |
### 6. DeliveryAgents Table Stores specialized logistical metadata for users operating as delivery personnel, utilized by the dispatch systems.
| Field Name | Data Type | Constraints | Description | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `agent_id` | BIGINT | PRIMARY KEY, AUTO_INCREMENT | Unique profile identifier. | | `user_id` | BIGINT | FOREIGN KEY (users.user_id) | Links to the core identity in the users table. | | `vehicle_type` | VARCHAR(50) | NOT NULL | e.g., "Bicycle", "Motorcycle", "Car". | | `is_online` | BOOLEAN | DEFAULT FALSE | Current working status for the dispatch algorithm. | | `is_verified` | BOOLEAN | DEFAULT FALSE | Admin approval flag; restricts unapproved accounts. |
### Entity-Relationship Logic The database operates on a highly normalized relational model. The `Users` table acts as the central hub; a single User can have a one-to-one relationship with a `DeliveryAgent` profile, or a one-to-many relationship with `Restaurants` (if they own multiple branches). A Restaurant has a one-to-many relationship with `MenuItems`. The core operational node is the `Orders` table, which forms relationships with a User (who buys), a Restaurant (who cooks), and an Agent (who delivers). The `OrderItems` table serves as a mapping layer between Orders and MenuItems, capturing historical pricing data to ensure that if a restaurant updates a dish's price tomorrow, past receipts remain accurate and untampered.

# 17. IMPLEMENTATION AND SCREENSHOTS
## 17.1 User Login and Registration Page [Insert Screenshot Here — Login Page] The Login and Registration screen serves as the secure entry point for all platform users. ## 17.2 Consumer Home Dashboard [Insert Screenshot Here — Consumer Dashboard] This screen acts as the primary discovery interface for consumers seeking food options. The UI is rich and visually engaging, displaying a prominent search bar, horizontal scrolling categories (e.g., Pizza, Sushi, Vegan), and a responsive grid of Restaurant Cards featuring establishment images, ratings, and estimated delivery times. The user navigates this screen to filter culinary choices based on their current geographic location or specific cravings. These interactions trigger background Axios requests to the REST API, dynamically updating the React component state to filter the rendered list. No security checks happen here beyond verifying the user's session token. Selecting a specific restaurant card pushes the user to the detailed Restaurant Menu screen.
## 17.3 Restaurant Details and Menu Page [Insert Screenshot Here — Restaurant Menu Page] This screen provides a deep dive into a specific establishment's offerings. The top of the page features a large banner displaying the restaurant's branding, address, and operational status. Below, the menu is organized into collapsible categories containing individual dish cards with descriptions, prices, and "Add to Cart" buttons. The user evaluates the menu and clicks the add buttons to build their order. This action triggers the React Context API to update the global cart state in real-time, causing a floating cart summary or badge counter to update instantly. The frontend strictly validates that the user is not attempting to add items from two different restaurants simultaneously, prompting an alert if a conflict is detected.
## 17.4 Cart and Checkout Drawer [Insert Screenshot Here — Checkout Drawer] The Cart and Checkout interface is a dynamic side-drawer or dedicated page that summarizes the user's intended purchase. It displays a list of selected items with quantity modifiers (+/-), a breakdown of the subtotal, calculated taxes, dynamic delivery fees, and the final grand total. The user reviews their order here and clicks the final "Confirm Payment" button. This crucial action triggers the construction of the final order payload, which is dispatched to the backend `OrderController`. The backend then strictly validates the data via the `PricingEngineService` to prevent client-side price tampering. Upon successful database commitment, the user is transitioned out of the checkout flow and directed to the persistent Order Success and Tracking screen.
## 17.5 Real-Time Order Tracking Screen [Insert Screenshot Here — Order Tracking] This interface provides the consumer with post-purchase visibility and peace of mind. It features a prominent visual status bar indicating stages such as "Order Placed", "Preparing in Kitchen", "Out for Delivery", and "Delivered". The user passively monitors this screen to know when their food will arrive. Internally, this screen relies entirely on the WebSocket connection established with the Spring Boot server. Whenever the restaurant owner or delivery agent updates the order status on their respective portals, the backend publishes an event. The React frontend consumes this event and instantly animates the status bar forward. This ensures real-time accuracy and prevents the user from needing to manually refresh the browser.
## 17.6 Restaurant Partner Dashboard [Insert Screenshot Here — Restaurant Dashboard] The Partner Dashboard is a B2B interface exclusive to users with the `RESTAURANT_OWNER` role. UI elements include order summary cards, status toggle buttons (e.g., "Mark as Ready"), and menu inventory tables. The owner uses this screen to monitor kitchen operations and toggle the availability of dishes if ingredients run out. Clicking an order status button triggers a secured API call that updates the MySQL `orders` table and subsequently fires a WebSocket notification to the delivery and consumer channels. Robust backend authorization ensures owners can only view and modify data explicitly linked to their `restaurant_id`.
## 17.7 Delivery Agent Console [Insert Screenshot Here — Delivery Console] Designed primarily for mobile viewport dimensions, this screen equips delivery personnel with logistical tools. When the `DispatchService` assigns them a delivery, an alert card appears detailing pickup and drop-off locations. The agent clicks "Accept" to lock the order to their account, triggering a database update that links their `agent_id` to the order record. Subsequent clicks on "Picked Up" and "Delivered" push status updates through the WebSocket layer, concluding the transaction lifecycle while enforcing checks that the agent is indeed an approved platform member.
## 17.8 Global Admin Dashboard [Insert Screenshot Here — Admin Dashboard] The Admin Dashboard is the comprehensive command center for platform administrators. It is characterized by data-dense UI elements, including analytical charts summarizing total revenue, active orders, and tabular grids listing pending user verifications. The admin uses this interface to govern the platform, such as clicking an "Approve" button next to a new delivery agent's profile. This action triggers the `AdminService` to execute a critical backend process, updating the `is_verified` flag within the `DeliveryAgentProfile` table. This overrides previous pending states and definitively unblocks the agent, allowing them to go online. The screen operates under the strictest security clearance, ensuring only `ADMIN` roles can query these overarching endpoints.

# 18. CONCLUSION
The development of the **UrbanBites** platform represents the successful culmination of integrating modern frontend user interfaces with robust, enterprise-grade backend architectures to solve a complex logistical problem. Over the course of the project, a fully functional ecosystem was built utilizing React.js, Spring Boot, and MySQL. The system successfully achieved its primary objective: providing a unified, multi-role platform that seamlessly connects hungry consumers with local culinary businesses and independent delivery agents. By replacing fragmented, manual workflows with digitized, automated processes, the project successfully demonstrated how technology can drastically optimize the operational efficiency of the food service industry while delivering a highly transparent, real-time experience to the end-user.
Constructing an application of this magnitude presented several significant technical challenges that required deep architectural problem-solving. A notable hurdle involved ensuring synchronization between the frontend state and the backend source of truth during the checkout flow. This was resolved by implementing a dedicated `PricingEngineService` that recalculates all cart logic server-side, eliminating the risk of client-side manipulation. Furthermore, handling complex state updates across different user profiles required rigorous debugging; for instance, resolving issues within the `AdminService` where delivery agents remained in a "pending" state despite approval required a deep audit of the JPA persistence logic to ensure the `is_verified` flag was correctly committed to the database. Deployment also introduced challenges, specifically managing CORS policies and environment variables when bridging the Vercel frontend with the Render backend, which was successfully navigated to achieve a live production environment.
Ultimately, this project serves as a comprehensive testament to the practical application of full-stack software engineering principles taught within the academic coursework. It demonstrates a holistic understanding of the entire software development lifecycle—from relational database modeling and secure RESTful API design to dynamic frontend state management and cloud deployment. The resulting UrbanBites application is not merely a theoretical prototype, but a production-ready, scalable architecture. It stands as a solid foundation that is fully capable of handling real-world traffic and is structurally prepared for future enterprise-level enhancements.
---

## 1. Integration of Third-Party Payment Gateways Currently, the system models the checkout flow but requires integration with live financial processors. The immediate future scope involves implementing webhook integrations with enterprise payment gateways such as Stripe or Razorpay. This would involve utilizing Python-based machine learning microservices or integrating with external AI APIs to analyze a user's historical order data, preferred cuisines, and ordering times. The backend would aggregate this data and provide personalized "Suggested for You" carousels on the React frontend. This feature adds immense value by reducing consumer decision fatigue and intelligently driving higher conversion rates for platform partners.
## 3. Advanced Geospatial Delivery Routing The logistical dispatch module can be significantly upgraded by incorporating advanced geospatial algorithms. Technically, this would entail integrating the Google Maps Routes API directly into the backend `DispatchService`. Instead of simply matching the closest agent based on raw distance, the algorithm would calculate optimal routing based on real-time traffic conditions, enabling batching of multiple orders along a similar trajectory. This enhancement would drastically reduce delivery times and minimize fuel expenditure, maximizing operational profitability.

The project can be expanded by integrating an advanced analytics dashboard for Restaurant Owners and Admins. This would involve utilizing complex SQL aggregation queries and potentially a NoSQL caching layer (like Redis) to process vast amounts of historical data without slowing down the primary transactional database. # 5. SYNOPSIS
**<u>SYNOPSIS</u>** This synopsis presents the purpose, objectives, and overview of the Food Delivery Application (UrbanBites) based on the implemented system.
## 5.1 Title of Project Food Delivery Application (UrbanBites)
## 5.2 Introduction The contemporary demand for online meal ordering has grown rapidly due to busy urban lifestyles, increased smartphone usage, and expectations of instant service. Consumers now require platforms that help them discover nearby restaurants, place orders quickly, and track deliveries in real time. However, traditional restaurant operations and fragmented delivery models lack proper synchronization, leading to delayed fulfillment and inconsistent customer experiences. Many existing systems also restrict restaurant owners from managing menus and orders with flexibility while limiting the visibility of delivery operations.
The Food Delivery Application (UrbanBites) addresses these limitations by providing a unified platform for consumers, restaurant partners, delivery agents, and administrators. The system enables restaurant discovery based on location, dynamic menu browsing, cart management, checkout with price verification, and delivery tracking. It supports role-based access control so that each stakeholder uses a dedicated interface with appropriate permissions. The result is a cohesive workflow that reduces delays, improves transparency, and strengthens the overall operational pipeline from order placement to delivery completion.
UrbanBites is designed using a layered architecture built on React for the frontend and Spring Boot for the backend. It integrates real-time updates through WebSockets, structured persistence through PostgreSQL, and scalable service components for dispatch and tracking. The project is intended for end consumers who expect seamless digital ordering, restaurant owners who need reliable order management and menu control, and delivery agents who require accurate routing and live status updates.
## 5.3 Objectives - To build a secure role-based authentication and authorization system for multiple user categories. - To implement location-aware restaurant discovery with search and filter capabilities. - To design a responsive menu and cart interface with consistent state management. - To enforce server-side price verification to prevent client-side manipulation. - To support real-time order status updates through WebSockets. - To enable a restaurant dashboard for menu management and order workflow control. - To create a delivery agent module for assignment, pickup, and delivery updates. - To provide a comprehensive admin panel for approvals, disputes, and platform governance. - To integrate secure payment processing and refund management flows. - To maintain accurate notifications and audit trails for critical actions. - To support geo-serviceability through service zones and location validation. - To ensure data integrity through a normalized relational database design.
---
# 6. FEATURES AND FUNCTIONALITIES
**<u>FEATURES AND FUNCTIONALITIES</u>** The following features are derived from the current backend and frontend implementation and are explained with technical context and user benefit.
## 6.1 Role-Based Authentication and Authorization The platform provides secure login and registration for multiple roles including Customer, Restaurant Owner, Delivery Agent, and Admin. Internally, Spring Security validates credentials and issues JWT access and refresh tokens with role claims. The frontend stores tokens and attaches them to API requests through an Axios interceptor, enabling protected navigation and API access. This feature ensures that sensitive operations such as approvals, menu management, and dispatch actions remain accessible only to authorized users.
## 6.2 OTP-Enabled Verification and Password Recovery UrbanBites includes OTP workflows for phone verification, login, and password reset. OTP codes are stored with expiry, attempt count, and lockout data to prevent abuse. Email OTP delivery is handled through SMTP templates, while SMS delivery is supported through a mock service for future integration. This provides a secure and user-friendly recovery mechanism without weakening account security.
## 6.3 Location-Based Restaurant Discovery Customers can discover nearby restaurants using location inputs and service-zone rules. The backend queries restaurant and service zone tables with geographic constraints, while the frontend uses map-aware interfaces for discovery. Filters such as veg/non-veg, price range, and rating can be applied to narrow the results. This feature improves relevance for the user and ensures only serviceable restaurants are displayed.
## 6.4 Menu Browsing and Category Organization Each restaurant maintains a digital menu with categories, pricing, and availability flags. Restaurant owners can add, edit, or disable items, and the public menu listing reflects only active items. Category tags allow structured browsing and faster selection. This feature reduces user effort during ordering and gives owners full control over their offerings.
## 6.5 Cart Management with Single-Restaurant Enforcement The cart module ensures that items from only one restaurant can be ordered at a time. When users add items, cart state is persisted via React state stores and validated on the backend. Cart items store a snapshot of prices and packing fees to maintain consistency. This constraint simplifies operations for restaurants and prevents cross-restaurant order conflicts.
## 6.6 Pricing Engine and Fee Breakdown The pricing engine recalculates delivery fees, platform fees, packing charges, and tax amounts on the server. Configurable rules include base fee, slab fee, per-km rate, surge multipliers, and minimum/maximum fee caps. The output is returned as a transparent breakdown on the checkout screen. This feature guarantees accurate billing and protects against client manipulation.
## 6.7 Order Placement and State Transitions The order service converts cart contents into an order with a pricing snapshot, item details, and delivery information. Order status progresses through defined states such as CREATED, PREPARING, and DELIVERED with validation for each transition. Owners and agents update status through role-protected endpoints, and cancellations are handled with refund workflows. This feature standardizes the order lifecycle and keeps all parties synchronized.
## 6.8 Payment and Refund Management UrbanBites supports Razorpay integration for payment creation and webhook verification. Payment records track provider IDs, idempotency keys, and status changes, including refund evidence and refund reasons. A mock payment flow is also available for local testing. This ensures that financial transactions are auditable and resilient to failures.
## 6.9 Dispatch and Delivery Assignment The dispatch module assigns orders to available delivery agents based on availability and status. Agents can accept or reject offers, and the system handles timeouts, reassignment, and no-agent scenarios. Dispatch events are recorded as a timeline for admin visibility. This feature automates logistics and reduces manual coordination effort.
## 6.10 Real-Time Tracking and ETA Updates Delivery tracking is supported through location pings and ETA calculations. Tracking updates are published to clients through WebSockets, enabling live order status screens. A MongoDB collection is defined for tracking points to support scalable time-series storage, with PostgreSQL storing current order state. This feature provides transparency and reduces customer uncertainty during delivery.
## 6.11 Notifications and Communication Users receive in-app notifications for key events such as order confirmation, delivery status changes, and approval decisions. Notification jobs maintain retries and delivery metadata. Email notifications use SMTP templates, and push/SMS senders are designed for future activation. This feature keeps users informed and improves operational reliability.
## 6.12 Administrative Governance and Approval Workflow Admins can manage platform operations such as approving restaurants and delivery agents, resolving disputes, updating pricing rules, and controlling payouts. Administrative actions are audited for accountability. This feature ensures platform safety, consistency, and regulatory compliance.
## 6.13 Media Uploads and Image Management This feature enables users and restaurant owners to upload profile pictures and menu images. The backend exposes multipart endpoints through the image handling controller, which validates file type and size before saving to local storage or Cloudinary based on configuration. The uploaded image path is stored against the relevant entity such as `users` or `menu_items`, ensuring persistent media references. This improves the overall user experience by making restaurant listings visually informative and professionally presented.
## 6.14 Approval and Compliance Workflow Partner onboarding is gated by approval status checks for restaurant owners, delivery agents, and restaurants. # 9. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
**<u>SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE</u>** UrbanBites follows a layered monolithic architecture with clear separation of concerns.
## 9.1 Presentation Layer The presentation layer is built with React.js and Tailwind CSS. It manages the UI for customers, restaurant owners, delivery agents, and administrators. It handles routing, form input, and state management using React Query and Zustand. This layer provides a responsive user experience across devices while sending HTTP requests and receiving WebSocket events.
## 9.2 Controller Layer The controller layer is implemented using Spring Web MVC annotations and maps HTTP requests to specific endpoints. Controllers validate request payloads, enforce role-based access, and pass data to service classes. This layer acts as the entry point for all API operations such as authentication, menu updates, and dispatch actions.
## 9.3 Service Layer The service layer encapsulates business logic and domain rules. Services coordinate pricing calculations, order transitions, dispatch decisions, and notifications. They also enforce constraints such as single-restaurant carts and approval gating. This layer ensures that core logic is testable and reusable across controllers.
## 9.4 Data Access Layer The data access layer uses Spring Data JPA repositories to interact with PostgreSQL. It abstracts SQL queries and allows mapping between Java entities and database tables. Complex queries are expressed through repository methods and annotations, ensuring clean separation from business logic.
## 9.5 Database Layer PostgreSQL stores persistent data including users, restaurants, orders, payments, and dispatch records. It enforces foreign keys, unique constraints, and indexes to maintain integrity and performance. MongoDB is configured for storing high-volume tracking points to support scalable delivery tracking.
## 9.6 External Services Layer External integrations include Razorpay for payments, Cloudinary for image uploads, OpenStreetMap Nominatim for geocoding, and SMTP for email notifications. WebSocket brokers provide real-time communication between the backend and clients.
## 9.7 End-to-End Request Flow When a user places an order, the React client sends a POST request to the order endpoint with cart details and a JWT token. The controller validates the request and calls the order service, which recalculates pricing, writes order and order item records to PostgreSQL, and triggers a dispatch workflow. The service then publishes a WebSocket event for the restaurant dashboard and returns an order confirmation response. The client updates the UI to show the tracking screen, while subsequent updates are pushed through WebSockets and persisted as tracking points.

## 16.28 Entity Relationship Overview The ER model uses `users` as the central identity table. Users can own restaurants, place orders, and act as delivery agents. Restaurants contain many menu items and are linked to service zones for delivery coverage. Orders connect users and restaurants and are composed of multiple order items. Payments have a one-to-one relationship with orders. Delivery agents are assigned through dispatch assignments and logged through dispatch events. Notifications and admin audits form supporting tables for communication and governance. Tracking points are stored separately in MongoDB for scalable location updates.

The checkout service would compute discount totals with these eligibility rules. This enhancement would improve marketing flexibility and increase user retention.

This feature would increase transparency and help users make informed choices.
## 19.3 Redis-Based Rate Limiting and Caching Introducing Redis can improve performance and security by enabling rate limiting for OTP requests and caching frequently accessed data. JWT blacklist checks can be optimized using Redis instead of database queries. This would reduce latency and strengthen protection against abusive traffic. The system is already structured to integrate this layer.
## 19.4 Advanced Geospatial Routing Integration with advanced routing APIs can improve delivery optimization. Instead of simple distance calculations, the system could use live traffic-aware routes to assign the best delivery agent. This would require extending the dispatch service with routing data and additional metadata storage. Faster delivery and better agent utilization would be achieved.
## 19.5 Analytics and Business Intelligence A dedicated analytics module can provide dashboards for restaurant owners and admins. This would aggregate order history, revenue trends, and peak time statistics. Data warehousing or caching could be introduced to avoid load on the primary database. Enhanced analytics would improve strategic decision-making.
## 19.6 Customer Support Automation An AI-based chatbot can be introduced to address common customer queries such as order status, refunds, or account issues. It would integrate with existing order APIs and escalate complex cases to human support. This would reduce support overhead and improve response time.
## 19.7 Advanced Monitoring and Observability A future enhancement involves centralized logging and performance monitoring for API requests, database queries, and WebSocket events. This could be implemented using tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and structured logging in the Spring Boot application. Such an enhancement would enable proactive detection of bottlenecks and improve system reliability. It would also provide actionable dashboards for operational analytics.

# 21. TESTING AND VALIDATION
**<u>TESTING AND VALIDATION</u>** This section documents how the system was tested to verify correctness, security, and stability across modules.
## 21.1 Unit Testing Unit tests focus on service-layer logic such as pricing calculations, OTP verification rules, and status transitions. Tests validate boundary conditions including empty carts, invalid OTP attempts, and incorrect role access. These tests are designed to ensure deterministic logic under controlled conditions. Unit testing improves confidence in core business rules and reduces regression risk.
## 21.2 Integration Testing Integration tests validate end-to-end workflows such as registration, order placement, and payment simulation. These tests exercise controllers, service layers, and persistence together to ensure correct data flow. In-memory H2 configurations can be used to run tests without external dependencies. This approach verifies that APIs behave correctly under realistic usage scenarios.
## 21.3 Security and Validation Testing Security testing includes verifying authentication filters, JWT validation, and role-based endpoint restrictions. Input validation tests confirm that invalid payloads are rejected with appropriate errors. OTP lockout and cooldown logic is validated to prevent brute-force attempts. This ensures that security-critical flows remain protected and consistent.
## 21.4 Manual UI Testing Manual UI testing validates the user experience across roles, ensuring that dashboards render correctly and API errors are handled gracefully. This includes testing cart flow, order tracking, menu management, and admin approvals. UI testing also checks responsiveness for mobile and desktop breakpoints. Manual verification ensures that the system remains intuitive and stable for real users.

# 22. DEPLOYMENT DETAILS
**<u>DEPLOYMENT DETAILS</u>** This section documents the typical deployment configuration for the frontend and backend components.
## 22.1 Frontend Deployment The React frontend can be deployed using modern hosting providers such as Vercel. Build artifacts are generated through Vite, and environment variables such as API base URLs are configured at deploy time. The deployment pipeline includes automated builds on each commit. This ensures fast delivery of UI changes and consistent hosting performance.
## 22.2 Backend Deployment The Spring Boot backend can be deployed on cloud platforms such as Render or any Java-compatible server. It requires environment variables for database credentials, JWT secrets, and SMTP configuration. Flyway migrations execute at startup to ensure schema consistency. This deployment flow maintains reliable API availability and database integrity.
## 22.3 Database Deployment PostgreSQL is deployed as the primary relational database with production-grade backups and access controls. MongoDB is optionally deployed for high-volume tracking storage. Connection URIs and authentication secrets are managed as environment variables. This ensures secure, scalable persistence across all modules.

# 23. MAINTENANCE PLAN
**<u>MAINTENANCE PLAN</u>** This section outlines the long-term maintenance approach for the system.
## 23.1 Monitoring and Logging Server logs should be captured and stored to trace errors, performance bottlenecks, and suspicious access. Structured logging with correlation IDs can simplify root-cause analysis. This practice ensures rapid resolution of production issues.
## 23.2 Database Backup and Recovery Scheduled backups of PostgreSQL should be performed to prevent data loss. Recovery procedures must be tested periodically to ensure data integrity. This protects critical transactional records such as orders and payments.
## 23.3 Security Updates Dependencies such as Spring Boot and frontend libraries should be updated regularly to address vulnerabilities. JWT secrets should be rotated periodically, and audit logs should be reviewed for anomalous behavior. This maintains platform security and compliance.
## 23.4 Performance Optimization As usage grows, caching strategies (Redis) and query optimizations can be applied. Slow endpoints should be profiled and optimized at the service and repository layers. This keeps user experience responsive under high load.
